newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen slumps as U.S. comments fan trade worry.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen slumps as U.S. comments fan trade worry.

text.p: The dollar slumped to its lowest levels in almost seven months against the yen amid concern a burgeoning Japanese current account surplus will fuel trade tensions between the U.S. and Japan.
Such worries were triggered after U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth.

His remarks came after a report showed Japan's current account surplus leapt 92.7 percent to 1.09 trillion yen in April from a year earlier and its trade surplus surged 90.9 percent to 1.02 trillion yen.

"The figures were pretty much in line with expectations but what hit the market was Summer's comments," said Steve Hannah, the director of research at IBJ. "The U.S. seems to be stepping up the war of words and it looks like we are going to test the 110 (yen) levels."

The dollar fell to 110.70 yen traders said, the weakest it has been since November 18, 1996. It was last at 110.88/98 yen at 0750 GMT from 112.43/53 late Tuesday in Europe. Dollar/mark was dragged lower in its wake and was at 1.7083/88 from 1.7188/93 Tuesday. The mark tumbled to 64.69 yen, its weakest since August 1995. It was at 64.88/91 from 65.41/44 Wednesday.

An official at Japan's Ministry of Finance said Wednesday that while the decline the Japan's trade and services surplus is slowing, the surplus was unlikely to rise significantly in the medium to longer term.

This cut little ice with traders, who were keener to focus on Summers' comments and remarks made on Tuesday by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky. Barshefsky said the recent trend in Japan's trade balance was "disturbing." She also said that the Clinton administration had told Japan it did not expect to see any significant increase in Japan's current account surplus.

Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and Eisuke Sakakibara, the director general of the Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said excessive yen strength or weakness was undesirable. Mitsuzuka also said Japan will tackle excessive currency moves in an appropriate manner.
Such comments are proving less and less supportive for the dollar, though, and it is expected to revisit the 110-yen level it has managed to hold above since the end of September 1996.
"They keep saying they don't want excessive moves but the question is what are they going to do about it," said David Coleman, the chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
He said Japanese gross domestic product statistics released Friday could be the cue for another lurch lower in dollar/yen.
"The risk is dollar could fall back below 110 (yen) if we get a strong GDP number on which gets people talking about a Japanese rate hike," Coleman said.
Economists are looking for a 1.1 percent increase in GDP in the first quarter after the 1 percent rise seen in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Meantime, in Europe, the mark was bolstered by lingering concern about whether European economic and monetary union will be delayed.

The French government triggered such speculation after it asked on Monday for time to consider a budget stability pact which would require it to maintain fiscal discipline after it joins the European single currency.

The difficulties Germany and France face in getting their budget deficits down to qualify for EMU is also casting a shadow over the outlook for EMU, traders said. They focused on a report in France's Les Echos newspaper saying the French deficit could reach 3.3 to 3.8 percent of GDP in 1997. This is above the three percent level required of single currency entrants. - Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
